The question of whether intermittent fasting (IF) can slow aging is genuinely contested in the retrieved evidence. On one side, a New England Journal of Medicine review cited by [d1] reported that "studies in rats showed that intermittent fasting greatly increased their lifespans and slowed the aging process," and low-credibility sources [d8] and [d10] claim IF promotes DNA repair, reduces oxidative stress, and slows aging through autophagy. A peer-reviewed source [d3] also notes that "both intermittent and periodic fasting can increase lifespan, even when there is little or no overall decrease in calorie intake."

On the other side, multiple studies from the German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases (DZNE) and Helmholtz Munich, published in Nature Communications, found that IF "proved largely ineffective in their supposed impact on aging" when tested in mice using a comprehensive new measurement method [d4][d5][d6]. Researchers concluded that "there is no internal clock of aging that you can regulate with a simple switch" [d5][d6], and that "fasting had overall very little influence" on how mice aged [d7]. An earlier DZNE study similarly found "only limited evidence for a retardation of aging as a consequence of fasting" [d2], noting that extended lifespan may reflect reduced cancer incidence rather than slower aging per se [d2][d9].

In summary, while some earlier research and popular sources suggest IF may slow aging, the more recent and methodologically rigorous peer-reviewed studies [d2][d4][d5][d6] find little to no evidence that IF genuinely slows the aging process, as opposed to merely extending lifespan through disease-specific effects. The scientific community remains divided on this question, and the evidence does not yet support a definitive conclusion [d9].
